subtopic_detail: Distinguishing corticosteroid-induced mood elevation from a first manic episode during an asthma admission
stem:
You are the registrar asked to review a 34-year-old man on a respiratory ward. He was admitted 5 days ago with a severe asthma exacerbation and started on prednisolone 50 mg daily, which he is still taking.

Over the past 3 days he has slept about 2 hours a night, has been talking rapidly and continuously, and has told staff he has designed a business that will make him wealthy within the month. He has telephoned several former colleagues after midnight and has spent a large sum online.

He has no personal psychiatric history and no family history of bipolar disorder. He has taken short courses of oral corticosteroid twice before, each for 5 days, with no psychiatric symptoms. He denies substance use and a urine drug screen is negative. On examination speech is pressured with flight of ideas, mood is elevated and expansive, and there is no disorientation, no visual hallucination and no fluctuation in attention. Sodium, calcium, glucose, thyroid function, full blood count and C-reactive protein are within normal limits or improving, and his asthma is now well controlled.

data_table.Examination: Pressured speech with flight of ideas, elevated and expansive mood, oriented, attention sustained, no hallucinations
data_table.Investigations: Sodium, calcium, glucose, thyroid function, full blood count and C-reactive protein within normal limits or improving; urine drug screen negative
data_table.Medications: Prednisolone 50 mg daily for 5 days, continuing

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discuss corticosteroid dose reduction with the treating team and start an antipsychotic for symptom control
options.rationale: Manic symptoms emerging within days of high dose corticosteroid in someone with no psychiatric history are a substance-induced mood disturbance, and the primary treatment is to reduce or withdraw the causative agent as the respiratory condition allows. An antipsychotic provides symptom control during the taper, since symptoms persist for days to weeks after the steroid is reduced and the behaviour carries real financial and interpersonal risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Continue the corticosteroid unchanged and start lithium with a plan for long-term mood stabilisation
options.rationale: Committing to long-term mood stabilisation treats this as a primary bipolar disorder when the temporal relationship to a known precipitant has not yet been tested by withdrawing it. Lithium would be appropriate if manic episodes recurred independently of corticosteroid exposure. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guidelines

options.text: Continue the corticosteroid unchanged and start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor for mood symptoms
options.rationale: Antidepressants can precipitate or worsen manic symptoms and have no role in an elevated mood state. They would be considered for the depressive phase that sometimes follows corticosteroid withdrawal, not for the manic phase. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Order magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and defer treatment until the imaging result is available
options.rationale: Structural imaging is warranted for first-episode mania with focal neurological signs, atypical age of onset or altered consciousness, none of which is present alongside an obvious pharmacological precipitant. Deferring treatment also leaves the disinhibited spending and calling unaddressed. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guidelines

options.text: Treat as hyperactive delirium with reorientation measures and regular review of attention and orientation
options.rationale: Hyperactive delirium features impaired attention, disorientation and a fluctuating course, and this man is oriented with sustained attention and a sustained elevation of mood. Delirium management would be correct if attention were impaired and the picture waxed and waned across the day. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Corticosteroid-induced psychiatric disturbance is common, dose-related and frequently missed because the patient is on a medical ward being treated for something else. Risk rises substantially above prednisolone 40 mg daily, symptoms typically appear within the first week, and elevated mood, irritability and insomnia predominate on initiation, whereas depressive symptoms are more characteristic of prolonged therapy or withdrawal. The absence of any prior psychiatric history, of family history and of previous reaction to lower-dose courses does not exclude the diagnosis, since the reaction is dose-dependent rather than idiosyncratic. Management is a negotiation with the treating team, because the corticosteroid is often genuinely needed, and symptom control with an antipsychotic buys time while the dose is reduced. Documenting the reaction matters for the future, since recurrence on re-exposure at similar doses is likely and prophylaxis can be planned.
key_points: Risk rises markedly above prednisolone 40 mg daily, with onset usually in the first week
Mania and irritability predominate on initiation; depression is more typical of prolonged use or withdrawal
Reducing or withdrawing the corticosteroid is the primary treatment where the medical condition allows
Antipsychotics give symptom control during the taper; antidepressants can worsen the elevated phase
Sustained attention and orientation distinguish this from hyperactive delirium
explanation.pearls: Symptoms usually resolve within about 6 weeks of stopping the corticosteroid, so document the reaction clearly in the record, since re-exposure at a similar dose carries a high risk of recurrence and may warrant prophylactic cover.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guidelines

subtopic_detail: Pharmacological choice for persistent aggression months after a moderate traumatic brain injury
stem:
You are the registrar in a rehabilitation unit. A 29-year-old man is 5 months post a moderate traumatic brain injury sustained in a motorcycle crash, with bifrontal contusions documented on imaging at the time.

He has made good physical recovery and walks independently. Nursing staff report that several times a week he shouts, throws objects and has twice pushed a staff member during personal care, settling within minutes and afterward expressing genuine regret.

Structured observation shows the outbursts cluster during morning washing and when his routine changes unexpectedly, and a behavioural support plan with consistent staffing and forewarning of transitions has been in place for 6 weeks with partial benefit. He has no pain on examination, is not constipated, has no urinary retention, and sleeps well. Mood is euthymic between episodes and he denies low mood, and he has no delusions or hallucinations. Sodium, calcium, thyroid function, full blood count and C-reactive protein are within normal limits, and an electroencephalogram shows no epileptiform activity.

data_table.Examination: Walks independently, no pain, not constipated, no urinary retention, euthymic between episodes, no delusions or hallucinations
data_table.Investigations: Sodium, calcium, thyroid function, full blood count and C-reactive protein within normal limits; electroencephalogram shows no epileptiform activity
data_table.Behavioural: Outbursts several times weekly clustering at morning washing and unexpected routine change; behavioural support plan in place 6 weeks with partial benefit

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological treatment to add?

options.text: Risperidone, titrated upward with monitoring of metabolic parameters and movement side effects
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are widely used but animal and clinical data suggest dopamine blockade may impair motor and cognitive recovery after brain injury, and sedation compromises rehabilitation participation. Risperidone would be reserved for aggression driven by psychotic symptoms, which are absent here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Propranolol, titrated upward with monitoring of pulse rate and blood pressure
options.rationale: Beta blockade has the strongest evidence base of any drug class for aggression following traumatic brain injury, and it is added here because a properly implemented behavioural plan has given only partial benefit. It is preferred over sedating alternatives because it does not impair the arousal and attention on which ongoing rehabilitation depends. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Diazepam, titrated upward with monitoring of sedation and respiratory rate
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines can cause paradoxical disinhibition in frontal lobe injury and impair the memory consolidation needed for new learning in rehabilitation. They have a role in brief acute sedation for immediate safety, not in ongoing management of recurrent outbursts. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Sodium valproate, titrated upward with monitoring of liver function and platelet count
options.rationale: Anticonvulsant mood stabilisers are sometimes used for post-injury agitation but the supporting evidence is weaker than for beta blockade, and the electroencephalogram shows no epileptiform activity to justify it on seizure grounds. Valproate would be more attractive if post-traumatic seizures coexisted. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Sertraline, titrated upward with monitoring of mood, sleep and gastrointestinal tolerance
options.rationale: Serotonergic antidepressants help where irritability arises from post-injury depression or emotional lability, and he is euthymic between episodes with no depressive symptoms. Sertraline would be appropriate if a depressive disorder were driving the irritability. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Aggression after traumatic brain injury is one of the strongest predictors of poor community reintegration and of carer breakdown, and it is usually the behaviour that determines whether someone can return home. Frontal injury impairs inhibition of responses to frustration, which is why outbursts are typically triggered, brief, followed by remorse, and clustered around specific care activities. Two steps precede any prescription: excluding treatable medical contributors such as pain, constipation, urinary retention, infection, sleep disruption and post-traumatic seizures, and implementing a structured behavioural plan, since environmental antecedents are modifiable and drugs cannot substitute for consistent handling. Where medication is needed, beta blockade is best supported, though often at doses higher than those used in cardiology and requiring several weeks for full effect. The overarching principle is to avoid agents that dull arousal, because rehabilitation gains depend on the patient being alert enough to participate.
key_points: Exclude pain, constipation, retention, infection, sleep disruption and seizures before prescribing
Implement a structured behavioural plan first, since triggers are identifiable and modifiable
Beta blockade has the strongest evidence for aggression after traumatic brain injury
Antipsychotics may impair motor and cognitive recovery and are reserved for psychotic drivers
Benzodiazepines risk paradoxical disinhibition and impair new learning
explanation.pearls: Propranolol for post-injury aggression often requires doses well above cardiac dosing and takes several weeks to show full benefit, so review pulse and blood pressure at each increment rather than abandoning it as ineffective at low dose.

sources.label: RANZCP: Neuropsychiatry of acquired brain injury
BMJ Best Practice: Traumatic brain injury

subtopic_detail: Recognising an immune cause of first-episode psychosis when catatonia and seizures follow a viral prodrome
stem:
You are the registrar in an emergency department. A 23-year-old woman is brought in by her parents with 3 weeks of increasingly disorganised behaviour, believing her housemates are broadcasting her thoughts online.

Her parents say she had a flu-like illness with headache a month ago, and that over the past week she has become withdrawn and at times holds odd postures for several minutes. She has no psychiatric history and no family history of psychosis. She uses no substances and a urine drug screen is negative.

Today in the department she had a witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 90 seconds. Since then staff have noted repetitive lip-smacking and choreiform movements of both hands that continue during periods when she is otherwise still. She is intermittently mute and resists passive movement of her limbs. Temperature is 37.9 °C. Non-contrast computed tomography of the brain is normal. Sodium, calcium, magnesium, glucose, thyroid function, liver and renal function are within normal limits, full blood count is normal and C-reactive protein is 12 mg/L (<5).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 148/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Intermittent mutism with resistance to passive movement, sustained odd posturing, orofacial lip-smacking and choreiform hand movements persisting at rest; witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 90 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Non-contrast computed tomography of the brain normal. Sodium, calcium, magnesium, glucose, thyroid, liver and renal function within normal limits; full blood count normal; C-reactive protein 12 mg/L (<5). Urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Formal electroencephalogram with a view to commencing an antiseizure medicine
options.rationale: An electroencephalogram is a reasonable adjunct and may show the extreme delta brush pattern, but it will not establish the cause and antiseizure treatment alone leaves the underlying process untreated. It would be the priority if the question were whether ongoing non-convulsive status was present. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Serum creatine kinase with a view to commencing treatment for neuroleptic malignant syndrome
options.rationale: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome requires exposure to a dopamine antagonist, and she has taken no antipsychotic medication, nor does she have the lead-pipe rigidity and marked hyperthermia typical of it. Creatine kinase would be central if she had received antipsychotics and developed rigidity with high fever. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Lumbar puncture with cerebrospinal fluid sent for neuronal surface antibody testing
options.rationale: Subacute psychosis with a viral prodrome, new seizures, orofacial dyskinesia, catatonia and autonomic instability in a young woman is the recognised presentation of anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor encephalitis, and cerebrospinal fluid antibody testing is the definitive investigation. Cerebrospinal fluid testing is specifically required because serum testing alone misses a meaningful proportion of cases. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Transvaginal pelvic ultrasound with a view to identifying an ovarian teratoma
options.rationale: Tumour screening is an essential part of management once the diagnosis is established, since an ovarian teratoma is found in a substantial minority of affected young women, but it follows rather than precedes antibody confirmation. It becomes the next step once cerebrospinal fluid antibodies return positive. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Serum caeruloplasmin with a view to identifying a disorder of copper metabolism
options.rationale: Wilson disease can present with psychiatric symptoms and movement abnormalities in this age group but evolves over months to years with hepatic involvement and Kayser-Fleischer rings, not over 3 weeks with seizures and fever. It would be worth testing in a subacute psychiatric presentation with tremor, dysarthria and deranged liver function. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor encephalitis characteristically begins with a viral-like prodrome and then produces psychiatric symptoms that are indistinguishable from a primary psychotic illness for days to weeks, which is why many patients are admitted to mental health units before the diagnosis is made. The features that should redirect thinking are neurological and autonomic rather than psychiatric: new seizures, orofacial dyskinesia, catatonia, autonomic instability and a decreased level of consciousness, particularly in a young woman with no psychiatric history. Standard investigations are frequently unremarkable, since computed tomography is typically normal, magnetic resonance imaging is normal in around half of cases, and inflammatory markers may be only mildly raised, so a normal first-line workup does not exclude it. Cerebrospinal fluid antibody testing is essential because serum testing alone has lower sensitivity and can be falsely negative. Treatment with corticosteroids, immunoglobulin or plasma exchange, plus removal of any associated teratoma, produces good recovery in the majority, and delay in immunotherapy is the strongest modifiable predictor of a poor outcome.
key_points: A viral prodrome followed by subacute psychosis, seizures, dyskinesia and catatonia is the characteristic sequence
Computed tomography is normal and magnetic resonance imaging is normal in roughly half of cases
Cerebrospinal fluid antibody testing is required, since serum testing alone misses cases
Ovarian teratoma is present in a substantial minority of affected young women and must be sought
Time to immunotherapy is the strongest modifiable determinant of outcome
explanation.pearls: Orofacial dyskinesia persisting while the patient is otherwise still is the single most discriminating bedside sign, because it does not occur in primary psychotic illness in an antipsychotic-naive patient.

subtopic_detail: Investigation sequencing for progressive dysphagia to solids and liquids with a normal endoscopy
stem:
You are the resident in a gastroenterology clinic. A 41-year-old woman describes 14 months of food sticking behind the sternum, now occurring with both solid food and drinks including water.

She regurgitates undigested food onto her pillow at night and has started sleeping propped up. She has lost 5 kg over the past year. She has taken a proton pump inhibitor at full dose for 6 months with no benefit, and says antacids have never helped.

She has no odynophagia, no haematemesis and no hoarseness. She has never smoked and drinks minimal alcohol. On examination she is thin with a body mass index of 19.2 kg/m2, the chest is clear and there is no lymphadenopathy. Gastroscopy performed last week was reported as showing a normal oesophageal mucosa with no stricture and no mass, with mild resistance passing the scope through the gastro-oesophageal junction that yielded with gentle pressure. Oesophageal biopsies showed fewer than 5 eosinophils per high power field.

data_table.Anthropometry: Body mass index 19.2 kg/m2, 5 kg weight loss over 12 months
data_table.Investigations: Gastroscopy: normal oesophageal mucosa, no stricture or mass, mild resistance at the gastro-oesophageal junction yielding to gentle pressure. Oesophageal biopsies fewer than 5 eosinophils per high power field

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat gastroscopy with dilatation of the gastro-oesophageal junction under direct vision
options.rationale: Empirical dilatation treats a presumed structural narrowing, and the endoscopy specifically found no stricture, so this intervenes before the mechanism is known. Dilatation would be appropriate for a confirmed peptic or fibrotic stricture causing solid food dysphagia. (Source: GESA: Dysphagia)

options.text: Ambulatory 24 hour oesophageal pH and impedance monitoring off acid suppression therapy
options.rationale: Reflux monitoring quantifies acid exposure in suspected gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, and her symptoms did not respond to full dose acid suppression and are not reflux-typical. It would be indicated for refractory heartburn or regurgitation where reflux remains the leading hypothesis. (Source: GESA: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease)

options.text: Computed tomography of the chest and abdomen with intravenous contrast to stage a suspected malignancy
options.rationale: Staging imaging follows a tissue diagnosis of malignancy, and endoscopy with biopsy has already excluded a mucosal lesion in the segment being imaged. It would be the next step if endoscopy had shown an infiltrating mass or ulcerated lesion. (Source: GESA: Dysphagia)

options.text: High resolution oesophageal manometry to characterise peristalsis and sphincter relaxation
options.rationale: Dysphagia to both solids and liquids from the outset points to a motility disorder rather than a mechanical obstruction, which typically begins with solids alone and progresses. With endoscopy having excluded mucosal and structural disease, manometry is the definitive test and is required to make the diagnosis and to subtype it. (Source: GESA: Dysphagia)

options.text: Videofluoroscopic swallow study with a speech pathologist to assess the oropharyngeal phase
options.rationale: Videofluoroscopy assesses oropharyngeal swallowing, which produces coughing, choking and nasal regurgitation at the moment of swallowing rather than food lodging retrosternally. It would be the right test for a patient with a neurological cause of transfer dysphagia. (Source: GESA: Dysphagia)

explanation.summary: The single most useful discriminator in dysphagia is whether solids alone or solids and liquids are affected, because mechanical obstruction narrows a lumen progressively and therefore troubles solids first, while a motility disorder disrupts coordinated transit and affects both from the outset. Nocturnal regurgitation of undigested food, weight loss and a complete lack of response to acid suppression all reinforce that picture here. Endoscopy remains the necessary first investigation in any adult with dysphagia because malignancy must be excluded and eosinophilic oesophagitis is now a common finding requiring biopsies even when the mucosa looks normal. A normal endoscopy in this setting is an informative result rather than a dead end, and high resolution manometry then classifies the disorder and, in achalasia, identifies the subtype that predicts response to pneumatic dilatation and to myotomy. Pseudoachalasia from a tumour infiltrating the gastro-oesophageal junction remains an important mimic, particularly with short symptom duration and rapid weight loss in an older patient.
key_points: Dysphagia to solids and liquids from the outset indicates a motility disorder
Solid food dysphagia progressing to liquids suggests mechanical narrowing
Endoscopy is the necessary first test to exclude malignancy and eosinophilic oesophagitis
Take oesophageal biopsies even when the mucosa appears normal
High resolution manometry is the definitive test and subtypes achalasia to guide treatment
explanation.pearls: Failure to respond to a full dose proton pump inhibitor trial in a patient with regurgitation should prompt manometry rather than dose escalation, because achalasia is regularly mislabelled as refractory reflux for years before the correct test is ordered.

subtopic_detail: Next therapeutic step after a proton pump inhibitor trial fails in oesophageal eosinophilia
stem:
You are the resident in a gastroenterology clinic. A 27-year-old man attends for review after an episode 3 months ago in which a piece of steak lodged in his oesophagus and required endoscopic removal.

He has a long history of asthma, hay fever and childhood eczema. He describes years of food sticking that he had adapted to by chewing extensively, cutting food finely and drinking water with every mouthful.

At the index endoscopy the oesophagus showed concentric rings and longitudinal furrows with white exudate, and biopsies from the proximal and distal oesophagus each showed 45 eosinophils per high power field. He was commenced on a proton pump inhibitor at full dose twice daily. A repeat endoscopy last week, after 10 weeks of therapy, shows persisting rings and furrows and biopsies showing 38 eosinophils per high power field. He reports no improvement in his swallowing.

data_table.Investigations: Index endoscopy: concentric rings, longitudinal furrows, white exudate; proximal and distal biopsies 45 eosinophils per high power field. Repeat endoscopy after 10 weeks of twice daily proton pump inhibitor: persisting rings and furrows, biopsies 38 eosinophils per high power field
data_table.History: Asthma, allergic rhinitis, childhood eczema; food impaction requiring endoscopic removal 3 months ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence a long acting inhaled corticosteroid by metered dose inhaler and repeat endoscopy after 8 to 12 weeks
options.rationale: The corticosteroid must be swallowed rather than inhaled so that it coats the oesophageal mucosa, and inhaled delivery sends the drug to the lungs where it does nothing for this condition. Inhaled delivery is correct for his asthma, which is a separate indication. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone at a weaning dose and repeat endoscopy with biopsies after 8 to 12 weeks
options.rationale: Systemic corticosteroid is effective but exposes a young man to cumulative toxicity for a chronic relapsing condition that topical therapy controls. Oral steroid is reserved for severe disease with malnutrition or stricturing requiring rapid control. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

options.text: Arrange skin prick testing to guide a targeted food elimination diet and repeat endoscopy after 8 to 12 weeks
options.rationale: Allergy testing predicts food triggers poorly in this condition, so elimination diets are structured empirically, most commonly by removing the six or the two most common trigger food groups. Dietary therapy is a legitimate alternative to topical steroid but should not be directed by skin prick results. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

options.text: Arrange endoscopic oesophageal dilatation and repeat endoscopy with biopsies after 8 to 12 weeks
options.rationale: Dilatation relieves fibrostenotic narrowing mechanically but does nothing for the underlying eosinophilic inflammation, which will continue to remodel the oesophagus. It is appropriate for a persistent stricture causing symptoms despite adequate anti-inflammatory therapy. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

options.text: Commence a swallowed topical corticosteroid preparation and repeat endoscopy with biopsies after 8 to 12 weeks
options.rationale: Persisting symptoms with more than 15 eosinophils per high power field after an adequate proton pump inhibitor trial confirms eosinophilic oesophagitis not responsive to acid suppression, and swallowed topical corticosteroid is the standard next-line therapy. Histological reassessment is required because symptoms correlate poorly with inflammation and untreated inflammation drives progressive fibrostenotic remodelling. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

explanation.summary: Eosinophilic oesophagitis is now the commonest cause of food impaction in young adults and is strongly associated with the atopic diathesis of asthma, rhinitis and eczema. The history of long-standing adaptive eating behaviour, such as chewing excessively, cutting food finely and drinking with every mouthful, is characteristic and frequently goes unreported unless asked about directly, because patients regard it as normal. Diagnosis requires at least 15 eosinophils per high power field on oesophageal biopsy with symptoms of oesophageal dysfunction, and biopsies must be taken from both proximal and distal oesophagus since the disease is patchy. Proton pump inhibitors are now understood as a treatment rather than a diagnostic filter, resolving inflammation in a meaningful proportion of patients, and non-response simply moves therapy along. The three established options are topical corticosteroids, dietary elimination and, in refractory disease, biologic therapy, with dilatation reserved for fixed strictures, and the treatment goal is histological remission because ongoing inflammation drives the fibrosis that ultimately causes strictures.
key_points: Suspect the diagnosis in any young adult with food impaction, especially with an atopic history
Diagnosis requires 15 or more eosinophils per high power field with oesophageal symptoms
Take biopsies from both proximal and distal oesophagus because involvement is patchy
Proton pump inhibitors are a treatment, not a diagnostic filter; non-response moves therapy on
Corticosteroid must be swallowed, not inhaled, and histological remission is the treatment target
explanation.pearls: Rinse the mouth and avoid eating or drinking for 30 minutes after a swallowed corticosteroid dose, because oesophageal candidiasis is the main adverse effect and adherence to that instruction largely prevents it.
